title: The hadran: goodbye to a book
hook: at the end of a tractate, a prayer: we will return to you, and you to us
carry: finishing a tractate is a promise to return
tomorrow: Berakhot opens with a clock. why does it close with peace?

segments.voice: Berakhot's last word was peace: they increase peace, builders, not winners. So the page is done. What do people do when the page runs out?

Last episode of a show you've watched for years. The credits roll and you don't reach for the remote. Now another room. A dining table, some chairs, a few old friends with big books open. Someone reads the last line of the last page, out loud. Bless His people with peace. Nobody closes the book. Instead they turn to a short paragraph printed after it, and start talking to the book itself.
screen: `THE CREDITS ROLL.` → `THE LAST LINE, OUT LOUD.` → `THEY TALK TO THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: It's called the hadran, after its first word, and it's said when a group or a person finishes a tractate of the Talmud. In plain words, it goes like this. We will return to you, tractate Berakhot, and you will return to us. Our mind is on you, and your mind is on us. We will not forget you, and you will not forget us, not in this world and not in the world to come. Listen to who's speaking to whom. A book is addressed like a friend at a train station. And the promise goes both ways. It isn't only we'll come back to you. It's you'll come back to us: the words will find us again, in a hard week, at a funeral, at a wedding toast, when we didn't go looking. Something to tell a friend tonight: the hadran goes on to read out a list of names, the sons of a sage called Rav Papa, and people have offered different reasons why, with no single answer. It's an odd, human thing to keep in a goodbye. The point isn't the list. It's that saying goodbye to a book is treated as a real goodbye, with feeling, and with a plan to meet again. Finishing isn't leaving. In the hadran, the last page is where you promise to come back to the first one.
screen: `HADRAN: WE WILL RETURN.` · `A BOOK, ADDRESSED LIKE A FRIEND.` · `YOU WILL RETURN TO US.` · `THE LAST PAGE PROMISES THE FIRST.` · then, large: `FINISHING A TRACTATE IS A PROMISE TO RETURN.`

segments.voice: Pick up one book that has mattered to you, any book, and hold it closed for a moment. Open it to any page and read a single line slowly. Then, out loud or in your head, tell it when you'll come back.
screen: `ONE BOOK THAT MATTERED.` · `ONE LINE, SLOWLY.` · `WHEN WILL YOU COME BACK?`

segments.voice: Hadran. Aramaic for we will return: the goodbye said to a finished tractate, with a promise both ways.
Pocket line: finishing a tractate is a promise to return, and the book returns to us. Forty-seven of fifty.

howItsDone: At a siyum, the completion of a tractate, the learners read its last lines and then say the hadran together, followed by a special Kaddish and a festive meal.

what a scholar hears: the hadran is post-Talmudic siyum liturgy; some also hear hadar, glory, in its first word ('our glory is on you'), and its list of Rav Papa's sons has several explanations.

tractate.meaning: one volume, or topic-book, of the Talmud

Rav Papa.meaning: a sage of the Talmud; the hadran lists his sons

Berakhot.meaning: the Talmud tractate about blessings and prayer
